comments.author: icyfox
comments.text:
Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):
- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.
- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.
- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.
- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.
- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back
Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

comments.author: x313
comments.text:
Many people here are assuming Nvidia committed some kind of crime that would've been exposed if not for government intervention. Yes the US govt is corrupt but they're likely right that there's no actual evidence. If there was, it would've already leaked from whoever's been leaking all the intelligence so far.
All of the stuff coming out has been pointing the other way. CIA/AG have both said they're unsure if the woman is a spy, US politicians briefed by intelligence have all said the same. Nvidia followed normal diligence in selling GPUs to a cloud provider in Southeast Asia (including visiting their data centers), then banned Megaspeed per government request in 2025. The idea that Nvidia knew they were smuggling hasn't been suggested by anyone involved in the actual investigations. Do people think Megaspeed told Jensen they were going to smuggle chips? What would be the possible benefit of this?
The Congressional committees will be about Nvidia did
enough
extra diligence. And there's no criminal investigation of Nvidia, only against Megaspeed, contrary to what everyone's saying.
The realistic risk for Nvidia isn't that executives get hauled off to jail for arguably weak diligence

comments.author: 015UUZn8aEvW
comments.text:
One of the takeaways from this, and from the 2023 OpenAI saga, is that a firm's nominal governance structure isn't necessarily its real governance structure.
Note that I'm not making any judgement about whether Huang or Altman
should
have been fired. The point is that in both cases, the board members were nominally empowered to make that decision, and did make it, rightly or wrongly. But when the rubber hit the road, it turned out that there were other forces that overruled them.
This means that we should have some skepticism about governance mechanisms that haven't been tested, such as the one that Anthropic has set up. The idea that board members will actually be able to carry out decisions that have massive negative ramifications for major stakeholders turns out to be questionable in practice.

comments.author: traceroute66
comments.text:
Its a cute idea but "drop-in replacement" is kind of overselling it if we are being totally honest here.
I certainly have no interest in supporting Microsoft, but ...
First you have the Outlook integration with Exchange.  Yes, in theory you can use IMAP with Outlook, but Microsoft are changing that with the new version of Outlook which also forces you to sync a copy of your IMAP mails to Microsoft.
Then you have the whole Office 365 bundle thing.  For one per-user price a month, you get Teams (internal + external voice calls and meetings) Email + Calendar (Outlook + Exchange), Office (Word + Excel), File Storage, Endpoint Management (Intune).
Then the reality that if you have 200, 2000, 20,000 staff who've spent their careers on Microsoft, you are not going to be wasting time with a "drop-in" replacement that isn't.  Its a lot of support load for already stretched IT teams.
So really, yes, technically Stalwart might be a drop-in replacement.  But in day-to-day practice, not so much....

We need a concrete counterproposal for how open-source models can proceed while mitigating these risks to acceptable levels.
For example:
1. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can find and exploit software vulnerabilities, how do we e.g. protect critical infrastructure around the world?
2. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can walk a non-chemist through the process of making nerve gas, how do we prevent nerve agent attacks?
3. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can help a non-biologist design a novel pathogen, how do we prevent the resulting pandemic?

I used to think GraphQL was a pretty good idea.   You can change the shape of your model, do complex queries, and ultimately switch out the backends.  What's not to love?
But over time I've come to realize that those features aren't all that helpful.  More fixed and static responses are much easier to manage.  They force the caller to do things in a performance oriented way for the backend.  And, importantly, all telemetry is based on CRUD/REST style endpoints.  You lose a lot of that if you just have a GraphQL endpoint.  It makes it supremely hard to see how you are being called or what you can drop.
It's flexible, but it adds too much undo complexity to a system that adopts it.
Well thought out REST endpoints organically grown as usage is required or observed trumps hyper flexible endpoints created because "Who knows what the user might need".  And particularly in the age of LLMs and AI where adding and deploying new endpoints can take hours rather than days.  Or making/updating a client for a service is extremely fast, there's just no reason not to go down that route.

I love the transparency, or at least given technical details, that Zhipu provide - a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs.

comments.author: aurareturn
comments.text:
For those wondering what loop transformers are:
LLMs have layers of data, called weights. During inference, each layer gets computed once. Moving weights from HBM memory to the chip is a major bottleneck because to generate a token, you need to move an entire layer into the chip, compute once, move it out, move the next layer in. Hence, memory bandwidth has been the #1 bottleneck for inference.
A loop transformer optimizes this bottleneck. Instead of one layer being computed once, it will compute the same layer multiple times, increasing the model intelligence without relying memory bandwidth as much. Bandwidth is still important, but not as much anymore.
More intelligence is squeezed by using the GPU compute that is typically sitting idle during inference.
